title: Mock Exam 3
instructions: Closed book, closed notes, no electronic devices. You have 70 minutes. Read every question fully before answering. Write all work you want graded on the FRONT of the page; the backs of pages are scrap and will not be graded. Provide only the number of examples/items a question asks for. For Big-O answers, give the tightest bound you know and justify it (a correct but loose bound earns no credit); say average case vs. worst case wherever it matters (especially for hashing). Use the TEXTBOOK (Weiss) version of every algorithm; a different but valid variant is graded as incorrect. Heaps use the textbook array layout (index 0 unused, root at index 1, children of i at 2i and 2i+1) unless a question says otherwise. Partitioning uses the textbook Section 7.7.2 Hoare method: swap the pivot with the last element, i starts at left and j at right-1, both i and j stop on elements equal to the pivot, and when they cross a[i] is swapped with the pivot. Array indices are 0-based unless stated. Code is C++11 or later using the standard library containers and algorithms; you are never asked to write a sorting algorithm yourself. Point values are shown next to each question.

questions.prompt:
**Question 1 (hash table trace, 14 points)**

A hash table uses **separate chaining**. It starts with TableSize = 5 and hash(x) = x mod TableSize. A new element is **appended to the end** of its bucket's list. Right after any insertion, if currentSize > TableSize (load factor above 1), the table is rehashed: the new size is the smallest prime that is at least twice the old size, and the old table is scanned from bucket 0 upward, each list from front to back, appending every element to its list in the new table. Insert, in this order:

**15, 26, 37, 41, 52, 64, 78, 93, 12, 86**

a) **(5 points)** One insertion triggers a rehash. Which one, and what is the new TableSize? Draw the table immediately after the rehash is finished (every bucket's list, in order).

b) **(5 points)** Draw the final table after all ten insertions.

c) **(2 points)** After these ten insertions, how many more insertions (of new keys) are needed before the next rehash, and what will the new TableSize be?

d) **(2 points)** What is the expected number of list nodes examined by an **unsuccessful** search in a chaining table with load factor lambda? What would happen to the cost of operations if this table were never rehashed while n grows?
questions.answer:
Engine-verified. Trace of the whole sequence (the line starting `REHASH` shows the re-insertion order):

```text

insert 15: hash = 15 mod 5 = 0 -> appended to bucket 0's list
insert 26: hash = 26 mod 5 = 1 -> appended to bucket 1's list
insert 37: hash = 37 mod 5 = 2 -> appended to bucket 2's list
insert 41: hash = 41 mod 5 = 1 -> appended to bucket 1's list
insert 52: hash = 52 mod 5 = 2 -> appended to bucket 2's list
insert 64: hash = 64 mod 5 = 4 -> appended to bucket 4's list
   load factor 6/5 > 1 -> rehash
   REHASH: new TableSize = nextPrime(2*5) = 11; re-inserting [15, 26, 41, 37, 52, 64] in old-table order with hash = x mod 11
insert 15: hash = 15 mod 11 = 4 -> appended to bucket 4's list
insert 26: hash = 26 mod 11 = 4 -> appended to bucket 4's list
insert 41: hash = 41 mod 11 = 8 -> appended to bucket 8's list
insert 37: hash = 37 mod 11 = 4 -> appended to bucket 4's list
insert 52: hash = 52 mod 11 = 8 -> appended to bucket 8's list
insert 64: hash = 64 mod 11 = 9 -> appended to bucket 9's list
insert 78: hash = 78 mod 11 = 1 -> appended to bucket 1's list
insert 93: hash = 93 mod 11 = 5 -> appended to bucket 5's list
insert 12: hash = 12 mod 11 = 1 -> appended to bucket 1's list
insert 86: hash = 86 mod 11 = 9 -> appended to bucket 9's list
  0: -
  1: 78 -> 12
  2: -
  3: -
  4: 15 -> 26 -> 37
  5: 93
  6: -
  7: -
  8: 41 -> 52
  9: 64 -> 86
 10: -
load factor 10/11 = 0.91
answer line: 1:[78,12] 4:[15,26,37] 5:[93] 8:[41,52] 9:[64,86]
```
**a)** The **6th insertion (64)** makes currentSize = 6 > 5, so the table is rehashed to nextPrime(2 x 5) = **11**. The old table, scanned in order, holds 15 | 26, 41 | 37, 52 | (empty) | 64, so the re-insertion order is 15, 26, 41, 37, 52, 64. The table right after the rehash (engine run on the first six keys):

```text
  0: -
  1: -
  2: -
  3: -
  4: 15 -> 26 -> 37
  5: -
  6: -
  7: -
  8: 41 -> 52
  9: 64

load factor 6/11 = 0.55
```
**b)** Final table (size 11): 1:[78, 12], 4:[15, 26, 37], 5:[93], 8:[41, 52], 9:[64, 86]. No second rehash (10 elements <= 11).

**c)** currentSize is 10 and the table has 11 buckets; the rehash happens when currentSize > 11, i.e. at the **12th element, so 2 more insertions**. New size: nextPrime(2 x 11 = 22) = **23**.

**d)** An unsuccessful search examines about **lambda** nodes on average (the bucket's list has length lambda on average), so it is O(1) while lambda <= 1. Without rehashing, lambda = n / TableSize grows linearly with n, so each list has length about n / 5 and every operation degrades to **O(n)**; rehashing keeps lambda near 1.

questions.prompt:
**Question 2 (heap trace, 10 points)**

The following is a **min-heap** in the textbook layout (index 0 unused and used for the value being inserted; positions 1 through 12):

`5  12  8  15  20  9  10  18  25  22  21  14`

Using the textbook **insert** (create a hole at the next free position, percolate it up while the new value is **strictly less** than the parent), insert the values **7, 3, 7, 2** in that order.

a) **(8 points)** For each insertion, show the path the hole takes (which parent values slide down) and write the heap array (positions 1 to n) after the insertion. Remember that the second 7 is equal to a value already in the heap.

b) **(2 points)** What are the worst-case and the average-case running times of one insert on a heap with n elements? When does the worst case happen?
questions.answer:
Engine-verified:

```text
min-heap insert 7,3,7,2
  [0]=7 | 5 12 8 15 20 9 10 18 25 22 21 14 _     # insert 7: hole created at index 13; 7 stored in index 0
  [0]=7 | 5 12 8 15 20 _ 10 18 25 22 21 14 9     # 7 < parent 9 (index 6) -> slide 9 down to index 13; hole moves to 6
  [0]=7 | 5 12 _ 15 20 8 10 18 25 22 21 14 9     # 7 < parent 8 (index 3) -> slide 8 down to index 6; hole moves to 3
  [0]=- | 5 12 7 15 20 8 10 18 25 22 21 14 9     # place 7 in index 3 (parent 5 is not larger)
  [0]=3 | 5 12 7 15 20 8 10 18 25 22 21 14 9 _   # insert 3: hole created at index 14; 3 stored in index 0
  [0]=3 | 5 12 7 15 20 8 _ 18 25 22 21 14 9 10   # 3 < parent 10 (index 7) -> slide 10 down to index 14; hole moves to 7
  [0]=3 | 5 12 _ 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10   # 3 < parent 7 (index 3) -> slide 7 down to index 7; hole moves to 3
  [0]=3 | _ 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10   # 3 < parent 5 (index 1) -> slide 5 down to index 3; hole moves to 1
  [0]=- | 3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10   # place 3 in index 1 (hole is the root)
  [0]=7 | 3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10 _ # insert 7: hole created at index 15; 7 stored in index 0
  [0]=- | 3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 # place 7 in index 15 (parent 7 is not larger)
  [0]=2 | 3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 _ # insert 2: hole created at index 16; 2 stored in index 0
  [0]=2 | 3 12 5 15 20 8 7 _ 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18 # 2 < parent 18 (index 8) -> slide 18 down to index 16; hole moves to 8
  [0]=2 | 3 12 5 _ 20 8 7 15 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18 # 2 < parent 15 (index 4) -> slide 15 down to index 8; hole moves to 4
  [0]=2 | 3 _ 5 12 20 8 7 15 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18 # 2 < parent 12 (index 2) -> slide 12 down to index 4; hole moves to 2
  [0]=2 | _ 3 5 12 20 8 7 15 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18 # 2 < parent 3 (index 1) -> slide 3 down to index 2; hole moves to 1
  [0]=- | 2 3 5 12 20 8 7 15 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18 # place 2 in index 1 (hole is the root)
final heap (from index 1): 2,3,5,12,20,8,7,15,25,22,21,14,9,10,7,18
```

**a)** Insert 7 (hole at 13): parent 9 slides down, parent 8 slides down, parent 5 is not larger -> `5 12 7 15 20 8 10 18 25 22 21 14 9`. Insert 3 (hole at 14): 10, 7, 5 slide down, 3 reaches the root -> `3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10`. Insert 7 (hole at 15): the parent (index 7) is also 7; 7 < 7 is false, so the hole stays -> `3 12 5 15 20 8 7 18 25 22 21 14 9 10 7`. Insert 2 (hole at 16): 18, 15, 12, 3 slide down and 2 reaches the root -> **2 3 5 12 20 8 7 15 25 22 21 14 9 10 7 18**.

**b)** Worst case **O(log n)**: the new value is smaller than everything and climbs the whole height of the tree (as 2 and 3 did). Average case **O(1)**: the textbook shows an insertion moves up only about 1.6 levels on average (2.607 comparisons), because most elements of a heap are near the bottom.

(2) insert 7: equal to its parent 7, strict < fails, stays at index 15

questions.prompt:
**Question 3 (heapsort trace, 8 points)**

Trace the textbook **heapsort** (Figure 7.10: a **0-indexed max-heap** inside the array, children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, buildHeap with percDown from i = n/2 - 1 down to 0, then swap a[0] with a[j] and percDown(a, 0, j) for j = n-1 down to 1) on:

`14  3  9  21  7  16  2  11  5  18`

a) **(3 points)** Show the array after each of the percDown calls of buildHeap, ending with the finished heap.

b) **(3 points)** Show the whole array after each of the first three deleteMax passes (bar between heap and sorted part).

c) **(2 points)** Why does heapsort use a **max**-heap to sort into ascending order? What order would the same procedure produce if a min-heap were used instead?
questions.answer:
Engine-verified:

```text
heapsort 14,3,9,21,7,16,2,11,5,18  (textbook Fig. 7.10: 0-indexed max-heap)
  14 3 9 21 7 16 2 11 5 18                 # start (n = 10); buildHeap: percDown from i = 4 down to 0 (MAX-heap, 0-indexed)
  14 3 9 21 18 16 2 11 5 7                 # buildHeap: after percDown(a, 4, 10) (value 7)
  14 3 9 21 18 16 2 11 5 7                 # buildHeap: after percDown(a, 3, 10) (value 21)
  14 3 16 21 18 9 2 11 5 7                 # buildHeap: after percDown(a, 2, 10) (value 9)
  14 21 16 11 18 9 2 3 5 7                 # buildHeap: after percDown(a, 1, 10) (value 3)
  21 18 16 11 14 9 2 3 5 7                 # buildHeap: after percDown(a, 0, 10) (value 14)
  21 18 16 11 14 9 2 3 5 7                 # == heap built ==
  18 14 16 11 7 9 2 3 5 21                 # deleteMax 21: swap a[0] with a[9], then percDown(a, 0, 9) -> heap = a[0..8], sorted = a[9..9]
  16 14 9 11 7 5 2 3 18 21                 # deleteMax 18: swap a[0] with a[8], then percDown(a, 0, 8) -> heap = a[0..7], sorted = a[8..9]
```
**a)** i = 4: `14 3 9 21 18 16 2 11 5 7`; i = 3: unchanged (21 is larger than its children); i = 2: `14 3 16 21 18 9 2 11 5 7`; i = 1: `14 21 16 11 18 9 2 3 5 7`; i = 0: **21 18 16 11 14 9 2 3 5 7**.

**b)** Pass 1: 18 14 16 11 7 9 2 3 5 | 21. Pass 2: 16 14 9 11 7 5 2 3 | 18 21. Pass 3: 14 11 9 3 7 5 2 | 16 18 21.

**c)** Each pass swaps the root with the last cell of the heap part; with a max-heap the root is the largest remaining element, which therefore lands in its final (rightmost) position, growing the sorted part from the right. A min-heap would put the smallest element in the last cell each time and produce the array in **descending** order.
rubric: (1) buildHeap starts at i = 4 and runs down to 0
(2) states after the percDown calls are correct (i = 4: ...18 ... 7; i = 2: 16 moves up; i = 1: 21 moves up; i = 0: finished heap 21 18 16 11 14 9 2 3 5 7)
(1) max-heap: the root is the largest element and goes to the last cell
(1) a min-heap would sort into descending order

questions.prompt:
**Question 5 (general knowledge, 2 points each, 8 points)**

Answer each part briefly (about two sentences each).

a) **(2 points)** A student implementing median-of-3 quicksort accidentally picks the **minimum** of a[left], a[center], a[right] instead of the median. Is the sort still correct? What happens to its efficiency, and on which kind of input is it worst?

b) **(2 points)** How many swaps of adjacent elements does insertion sort perform on `5 8 1 7 3 2`? What does the average number of inversions in an n-element array tell you about every sort that only swaps adjacent elements?

c) **(2 points)** What is the running time of counting sort on n integers that lie in the range 0 to k-1? When is it a poor choice, and why does it not violate the Omega(n log n) lower bound?

d) **(2 points)** `std::set` and `std::unordered_set` both implement the set ADT. Give the cost of insert and find for each (state average/worst for the hash version), and name one operation the ordered set supports that the hash set cannot do efficiently.
questions.answer:
**a)** It is still **correct**: any element is a valid pivot, partitioning still puts the pivot in its final place. But the pivot is never the median of the three (it is the smallest), so the splits are lopsided; on **already sorted** input the minimum of the three is a[left], so each partition peels off one element: T(n) = T(n-1) + cn = **O(n^2)**, the very case median-of-3 was meant to avoid. Even on random input the constant factor gets worse.

**b)** Insertion sort does one swap per inversion. The array `5 8 1 7 3 2` has **10 inversions** (engine: (5,1) (5,3) (5,2) (8,1) (8,7) (8,3) (8,2) (7,3) (7,2) (3,2)), so 10 adjacent swaps. The average number of inversions in a random permutation of n distinct elements is n(n-1)/4, and each adjacent swap removes at most one inversion, so every adjacent-swap sort needs **Omega(n^2)** swaps on average.

**c)** **O(n + k)**: one pass to count, one pass over the k counters, one pass to write out. It is poor when k is much larger than n (e.g. 32-bit keys, k = 2^32) or the keys are not small integers. It is not comparison-based (it uses the key as an array index), so the decision-tree lower bound does not apply.

**d)** `std::set` (balanced BST): insert and find **O(log n)** worst case. `std::unordered_set` (hash): insert and find **O(1) average, O(n) worst case**. The ordered set also supports ordered operations: smallest/largest element, in-order traversal, `lower_bound`/range queries, the predecessor/successor of a value; the hash set cannot do these without scanning O(n).


Engine check of part (b): `10 inversions: [(5, 1), (5, 3), (5, 2), (8, 1), (8, 7), (8, 3), (8, 2), (7, 3), (7, 2), (3, 2)]`
rubric: (1) still correct (any element is a valid pivot)
(1) efficiency: pivot is never the median; sorted input gives O(n^2) behavior again
(1) 10 adjacent swaps (= number of inversions)
(1) average n(n-1)/4 inversions, each adjacent swap removes one, so Omega(n^2) average for adjacent-swap sorts
(1) counting sort O(n + k)
(1) poor when k is large relative to n / keys not small integers; not comparison-based so the bound does not apply
(1) set O(log n) for insert/find; unordered_set O(1) average, O(n) worst
(1) names an ordered-only operation (min/max, in-order traversal, lower_bound, range query)

questions.prompt:
**Question 6 (design and analyze, 16 points)**

Numbers arrive from a sensor one at a time, **n** in total (you do not know n in advance). After **each** arrival the system must immediately report the **median** of all numbers received so far (for an even count, report the smaller of the two middle values).

a) **(3 points)** Describe two straightforward designs and give the **total** time each takes for all n arrivals and reports.

b) **(7 points)** Describe the design that is most efficient as measured by algorithmic time complexity. Name the data structures, the invariants you maintain, and exactly what you do for each arriving number and for each report. (Hint: heaps.)

c) **(4 points)** Fully analyze the total running time of your design for all n arrivals and reports, and its space.

d) **(2 points)** Show the contents of your data structures and the reported median after each of the numbers **5, 2, 8, 1** arrive.
questions.answer:
**a)** (1) Keep a sorted `vector`: each arrival is found by binary search in O(log n) but inserting shifts up to n elements, O(n); the report is O(1). Total **O(n^2)**. (2) Store everything in a vector and run quickselect for the middle element after each arrival: O(n) average per report, total **O(n^2)** average (O(n^3) worst case). (An ordered `set` does not help: it has no way to jump to the middle element, `std::next(begin(), n/2)` is O(n).)

**b)** Use **two heaps**: `lo`, a max-heap (`priority_queue<int>`) holding the smaller half of the numbers, and `hi`, a min-heap (`priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>`) holding the larger half. Invariants: (1) every element of `lo` is <= every element of `hi`; (2) `|lo| == |hi|` or `|lo| == |hi| + 1`.
- *Arrival of x*: if `lo` is empty or `x <= lo.top()` push x on `lo`, otherwise push it on `hi`. Then rebalance: if `|lo| > |hi| + 1`, move `lo.top()` to `hi`; else if `|hi| > |lo|`, move `hi.top()` to `lo`.
- *Report*: the median (the smaller middle value when the count is even) is `lo.top()`.

**c)** Each arrival does one push and at most one pop followed by one push, so a constant number of heap operations on heaps of at most n elements, each **O(log n)** worst case: O(log n) per arrival. A report is `top()`, **O(1)**. All n arrivals and reports: n * (O(log n) + O(1)) = **O(n log n)** worst case. Space **O(n)** (all numbers are stored). This beats the O(n^2) of part (a).

**d)**
| arrives | lo (max-heap) | hi (min-heap) | reported median |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | {5} | {} | 5 |
| 2 | {2} (5 moved to hi) | {5} | 2 |
| 8 | {5, 2} (5 moved back) | {8} | 5 |
| 1 | {2, 1} (5 moved to hi) | {5, 8} | 2 |
rubric: (1) design 1 (sorted vector with shifting inserts) with total O(n^2)
(1) design 2 (quickselect / sorting each time) with total O(n^2) (average)
(1) both reasoned as O(n) work per arrival
(2) two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half (types/directions correct)
(2) invariants: every element of lo <= every element of hi, and sizes differ by at most one with lo holding the extra
(2) arrival procedure: choose the heap by comparing to lo.top(), then rebalance by moving a top
(1) report is lo.top()
(1) each heap operation is O(log n) and an arrival uses a constant number of them
(1) total O(n log n) (n arrivals x O(log n), reports O(1))
(1) space O(n)
(1) report cost O(1) noted explicitly / consecutive costs combined correctly
(1) trace after 5 and 2: lo {5}, hi {}, median 5; then lo {2}, hi {5}, median 2
(1) trace after 8 and 1: medians 5 and 2 with the correct heap contents

questions.prompt:
**Question 7 (algorithm analysis, 10 points)**

You must find the **k-th largest** of n distinct integers stored in an unsorted vector (1 <= k <= n). Consider four algorithms from the course:

- **A**: sort the whole vector with `std::sort` and read the element at the right position.
- **B**: run buildHeap on all n elements (max-heap), then do deleteMax k times; the last one removed is the answer.
- **C**: keep a **min-heap of at most k elements**: for each of the n elements push it, and pop the minimum if the heap has more than k elements; the answer is the top at the end.
- **D**: textbook quickselect (median-of-3 pivot, Hoare partition).

a) **(7 points)** Give the tight running time of each in terms of n and k: A (worst case), B (worst case), C (worst case), D (average case **and** worst case). Justify B, C and D in a sentence each.

b) **(3 points)** Now let k = n/2 (the median). Simplify the bounds of B, C and D (average) to functions of n alone, and say which of the four is asymptotically best and why the two heap algorithms are no better than A.
questions.answer:
**a)**
- **A: O(n log n)**: introsort (std::sort) is O(n log n) worst case whatever k is.
- **B: O(n + k log n)**: buildHeap is O(n); each of the k deleteMax operations is O(log n) (heap size is at most n).
- **C: O(n log k)**: n iterations, and the heap never holds more than k + 1 elements, so each push/pop is O(log k).
- **D: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case**: each partition costs the size of the range and, on average, the range halves (n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n)); with consistently bad pivots it only shrinks by one each time.

**b)** For k = n/2: B = O(n + (n/2) log n) = **O(n log n)**; C = O(n log (n/2)) = **O(n log n)**; D average = **O(n)**. **D (quickselect)** is asymptotically best on average. The heap methods are no better than sorting because with k proportional to n they still perform Theta(n) heap operations of cost Theta(log n) each. (Only for small k, e.g. k = O(1) where B is O(n) and C is O(n), do the heaps beat sorting; D's worst case O(n^2) is the price for its speed.)
